replies.probe: What makes a working relationship reliable?
replies.a: For me, reliability comes from honesty, follow-through, and making room to speak when something goes wrong. Good work matters, but so does giving credit, explaining decisions, and treating people fairly—especially when plans change.
replies.b: For me, reliability is keeping the small agreements: sharing the right file, correcting mistakes, and updating people when plans change. Nobody has to make a big deal of it; it just means we can count on each other.

replies.probe: Two strategies offer similar gains. One is safe, the other riskier. How do you choose?
replies.a: I’d weigh how reversible the risky choice is and what happens if it fails. If the downside is limited and I can learn or recover, I’d lean toward taking it; if it could wipe out something important, I’d choose the safe option. Similar gains alone aren’t enough to justify a risk.
replies.b: I’d usually choose the safer one when the gains are similar. I’d take the riskier option only if the upside is meaningful to me, I can absorb the downside, and there’s a good reason to expect it to pay off.

replies.probe: Someone you work with makes a serious mistake and then refuses to own it. How do you respond?

If they still refused responsibility, I’d document the facts and raise it through the appropriate channel.
replies.b: I’d address the mistake directly and privately, focusing on what happened, its impact, and what needs to be fixed. If they still refused to take responsibility, I’d document the facts and raise it through the appropriate channel—not to punish them, but to make sure the issue gets resolved and doesn’t recur.
